dx: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease presenting as knee pain
case: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of a limp and intermittent pain in his right medial thigh and knee that worsens after play. He recalls no injury. He is at the 15th percentile for height. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). The right knee has full range of motion without swelling or tenderness. Abduction and internal rotation of the right hip are limited and painful. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 8 mm/h (0 to 20). Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral radiographs of the pelvis show a flattened, sclerotic, fragmented right femoral capital epiphysis with no displacement at the physis. Diagnosis: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease.

questions.stem: His 3-week-old sister is examined. With her right hip flexed and adducted, gentle backward pressure on the knee pushes the femoral head out of the acetabulum, and abducting the hip returns it with a palpable clunk. Which of the following best explains the sister's finding?
options: Idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral capital epiphysis
Shear failure through the hypertrophic zone of the physis
Shallow acetabulum with a lax hip joint capsule
Bacterial infection distending the hip joint capsule
approach: Recognize the maneuvers: backward pressure on the adducted hip dislocates it (Barlow), and abduction reduces it with a clunk (Ortolani).
A newborn with a hip that can be dislocated and reduced has developmental dysplasia of the hip.
Match it to its cause: a shallow acetabulum and a lax capsule that let the head slide out.
questions.why: The Barlow test (adduct and push back) dislocates an unstable hip, and the Ortolani test (abduct and lift) reduces it with a clunk. Positive tests in a newborn mean developmental dysplasia of the hip, where a shallow acetabulum and lax capsule fail to hold the femoral head. Each pediatric hip disorder has its own age group: dysplasia in newborns, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease at about 4 to 8 years, and slipped capital femoral epiphysis in obese adolescents.
whyNot: This describes Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, her brother's disorder. It appears at about 4 to 8 years of age and does not make a newborn hip dislocatable.
This describes slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which occurs in adolescents during the growth spurt, often with obesity.
Correct.
Septic arthritis of the hip causes fever, irritability, and refusal to move the leg. It does not produce a hip that slides out and back in with a clunk.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the femoral capital epiphysis of a child this age is especially vulnerable to infarction?
options: Its blood comes mainly from retinacular branches of one artery
It gets most of its blood through the artery in the ligament of the head
Its blood arrives through metaphyseal vessels crossing the open physis
Its marrow fat expands and compresses the sinusoids within the femoral head
approach: Avascular necrosis is a bone infarct, so ask where the blood supply comes from and how many routes it has.
In young children the growth plate blocks metaphyseal vessels, and the artery of the ligament of the head adds little.
That leaves the retinacular (lateral epiphyseal) branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery as nearly the only source.
questions.why: Avascular necrosis is infarction of bone after its blood supply is cut off. In a child of about 4 to 8 years, the femoral capital epiphysis depends almost entirely on retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery that run up the femoral neck. The open physis is a barrier to metaphyseal vessels, and the artery in the ligament of the head contributes little at this age. With essentially one route, any interruption can infarct the epiphysis. The femoral head is also the most common site of avascular necrosis in adults, for the same reason.
whyNot: Correct.
The artery in the ligament of the head is a small branch of the obturator artery. It supplies only a small area near the fovea and contributes little in young children.
The open physis acts as a barrier, so metaphyseal vessels do not cross it to supply the epiphysis in children.
Marrow fat enlargement compressing sinusoids is one proposed mechanism for glucocorticoid-related osteonecrosis in adults. It is not why a young child's femoral head is vulnerable.

topics: Blood supply of the femoral head

questions.stem: His pain is felt along the medial thigh above the knee, the cutaneous territory of one of the nerves that supply the hip joint. Based on Hilton law, this same nerve also supplies which of the following muscle groups?
options: Hamstrings in the posterior compartment of the thigh
Gluteus medius and minimus in the gluteal region
Short lateral rotators deep to the gluteus maximus
Adductors of the thigh in the medial compartment
approach: Identify the nerve: skin of the medial thigh is supplied by the cutaneous branch of the obturator nerve.
Apply Hilton law: a nerve that supplies a joint also supplies muscles that move that joint and the skin over them.
The obturator nerve supplies the hip joint and the adductors of the medial thigh.
questions.why: Hilton law states that the nerves supplying the muscles that act on a joint also supply the joint itself. The obturator nerve sends articular branches to the hip, motor branches to the adductor muscles of the medial thigh, and a cutaneous branch to the medial thigh. Pain from an irritated hip capsule travels in this nerve and is often felt in the medial thigh or knee, which is why a child with knee pain and a normal knee exam needs a hip exam.
whyNot: The hamstrings are supplied by the sciatic nerve (tibial part), which does not supply the skin of the medial thigh.
The gluteus medius and minimus are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, which has no cutaneous branch to the thigh.
The short lateral rotators get their own small nerves from the sacral plexus, not the nerve to the medial thigh skin.
Correct.

questions.stem: At 41 years of age, he has worsening right groin pain with walking. Radiographs show narrowing of the superior hip joint space, subchondral sclerosis, and marginal osteophytes around a flattened, enlarged femoral head. Which of the following best explains how the abnormal shape of his femoral head led to these changes?
options: Synovial pannus releasing enzymes that erode cartilage margins
Concentrated load inducing chondrocytes to release metalloproteinases
Autoantibodies against type II collagen fixing complement in cartilage
Neutrophil proteases released into the synovial fluid of the joint
approach: Recognize secondary osteoarthritis: joint space narrowing, sclerosis, and osteophytes in a joint with an old deformity.
A misshapen femoral head fits the acetabulum poorly, so load is concentrated on a small area of cartilage.
Stressed chondrocytes make matrix-degrading enzymes, and the matrix breaks down.
questions.why: Osteoarthritis begins in the cartilage itself. Abnormal or concentrated mechanical load injures chondrocytes, which respond by releasing matrix metalloproteinases (such as collagenase) and aggrecanases, partly driven by IL-1. These enzymes degrade type II collagen and aggrecan, so the cartilage loses proteoglycan, fibrillates, and wears away. Subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes follow as the bone responds to the changed load. Prior joint deformity or injury is a classic risk factor for this secondary osteoarthritis.
whyNot: Pannus is inflamed synovium that erodes cartilage and bone at the margins in rheumatoid arthritis. Osteoarthritis has little synovial inflammation.
Correct.
Antibodies to type II collagen are a feature of experimental models and some inflammatory arthritides, not of osteoarthritis after a childhood deformity.
Neutrophil proteases destroy cartilage quickly in septic arthritis. Osteoarthritic joint fluid is noninflammatory, with few neutrophils.

dx: Osgood-Schlatter disease in an adolescent soccer player
case: A 12-year-old girl who plays competitive soccer is brought to the physician because of a 3-month history of pain just below her right kneecap. The pain is worse with running, jumping, and kneeling and improves with rest. She has grown 7 cm in the past year. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F). The right tibial tubercle is prominent, swollen, and tender. Extension of the knee against resistance reproduces the pain. The knee is stable, and there is no effusion. A lateral radiograph of the knee shows soft tissue swelling and fragmentation of the tibial tubercle apophysis. Diagnosis: Osgood-Schlatter disease.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old teammate has vague right knee pain with episodes of the knee catching and locking. A tunnel-view radiograph shows a well-demarcated lucent lesion containing a bone fragment on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle. Which of the following best describes the teammate's disorder?
options: Softening and fissuring of the patellar articular cartilage
Traction apophysitis at the tibial tubercle insertion
Longitudinal tear of the medial meniscus at its periphery
Separation of a subchondral bone and cartilage fragment
approach: Note the findings: mechanical locking and a lesion with a bone fragment on the femoral condyle.
A lesion of subchondral bone with its cartilage, classically on the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle, is osteochondritis dissecans.
Compare with the other adolescent knee disorders, which involve the patella or the tibial tubercle.
questions.why: Osteochondritis dissecans is separation of a piece of subchondral bone and its overlying articular cartilage, most often from the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle. If the fragment loosens, it can catch or lock the knee. Osgood-Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, and chondromalacia patellae is softening of patellar cartilage with anterior knee pain. Each has a different location, so the site of the lesion sorts them.
whyNot: This is chondromalacia patellae. It causes anterior knee pain, often worse after sitting or on stairs, and does not show a condylar bone fragment.
This is Osgood-Schlatter disease, the girl's disorder. It affects the tibial tubercle, not the femoral condyle.
A meniscal tear can cause locking, but it is a soft tissue injury seen on MRI. It does not produce a lucent bony lesion with a fragment on radiographs.
Correct.

questions.stem: The tibial tubercle and the patellar tendon that pulls on it develop from the same embryonic tissue. Which of the following structures also arises from this tissue?
options: Ribs
Sternum
Mandible
Quadriceps femoris muscle fibers
approach: Identify the source: bones, cartilage, and tendons of the limbs come from the somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm.
Recall the other sources: the axial skeleton from sclerotome, limb muscle from somite myotomes, and most craniofacial bone from neural crest.
Find the structure built from the somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm in the body wall: the sternum.
questions.why: Limb bones, cartilage, ligaments, and tendons develop from the somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm. The sternum also forms from this layer, as paired sternal bars in the ventral body wall that fuse in the midline. By contrast, the vertebrae and ribs come from sclerotome, limb muscle fibers come from somite myotomes that migrate into the limb bud, and most craniofacial bone comes from neural crest mesenchyme.
whyNot: Ribs develop from the costal processes of thoracic vertebrae, which come from sclerotome of paraxial mesoderm.
Correct.
The mandible forms mainly from neural crest mesenchyme of the first pharyngeal arch.
Limb muscle fibers come from myogenic cells that migrate from somites into the limb bud, even though the tendons they attach to come from lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.stem: During rehabilitation, needle electromyography of her vastus lateralis is recorded as she slowly increases the force of knee extension. Small motor unit potentials appear first, and larger ones are added as force rises. Which of the following best explains this order?
options: Small motor neurons reach threshold with less synaptic current
Large motor neurons are held back by Renshaw cell inhibition at rest
Type II muscle fibers need more acetylcholine to reach threshold
Large motor units fire only after Golgi tendon organs signal tension
approach: Recognize the size principle: motor units are recruited from smallest to largest as force rises.
The order is set by the motor neurons, not the muscle fibers.
Small motor neurons have high input resistance, so a given synaptic current depolarizes them to threshold first.
questions.why: Muscle force is graded by recruiting more motor units and by raising their firing rate toward fused tetanus. Recruitment follows the size principle: small motor neurons, which supply small units of fatigue-resistant type I fibers, have a high input resistance and reach threshold with less synaptic input. Larger motor neurons with fast, powerful type II units join only as the descending drive grows. This gives fine control at low force and saves the fatigable units for strong efforts such as a hard kick.
whyNot: Correct.
Renshaw cells give recurrent inhibition to active motor neurons. They do not set the small-to-large recruitment order.
All skeletal muscle fiber types reach threshold reliably with each nerve impulse because the neuromuscular junction has a large safety factor. Recruitment order is set by the motor neurons.
Golgi tendon organs sense tension and inhibit the same muscle through Ib afferents. They do not trigger recruitment of large units.

topics: Size principle and motor unit recruitment

questions.stem: Two years later, she sustains a closed fracture of the right tibial shaft that is treated in a cast. At 3 weeks, the fracture gap is bridged by a cartilage-rich soft callus. Which of the following collagen types predominates in this callus, and which predominates in the bone that replaces it?
options: Type I, then type II
Type III, then type II
Type II, then type I
Type IV, then type I
approach: Place the time point in the healing sequence: hematoma and inflammation, then soft callus, then hard callus, then remodeling.
Soft callus is cartilage made by chondrocytes, so its main collagen is type II.
Hard callus is woven bone made by osteoblasts, so its main collagen is type I.
questions.why: A fracture heals in four overlapping stages: hematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, and remodeling. In the soft callus, mesenchymal cells become chondrocytes and lay down cartilage rich in type II collagen, which splints the fracture. Blood vessels then invade, the cartilage calcifies, and osteoblasts replace it with woven bone made of type I collagen (hard callus) by endochondral ossification. Remodeling later turns woven bone into lamellar bone. Poor blood supply, instability, infection, smoking, diabetes, and malnutrition delay this sequence.
whyNot: This reverses the order. Bone (type I) replaces cartilage (type II), not the other way around.
Type III collagen is typical of early granulation tissue in the hematoma, and bone does not replace it with type II collagen.
Correct.
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes. It is not the main collagen of a cartilage callus.

topics: Collagen types in cartilage and bone

dx: Acute hematogenous Staphylococcus aureus osteomyelitis of the distal tibia in a child
case: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of fever and increasing pain above his left ankle. He now refuses to bear weight on the left leg. Two weeks ago he had an infected scrape on his knee that healed. Temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. The distal left tibia is warm, swollen, and exquisitely tender. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3 (4,500 to 13,500), erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 72 mm/h (0 to 20), and C-reactive protein is 9.4 mg/dL (less than 1.0). MRI shows marrow edema and a small subperiosteal abscess at the distal tibial metaphysis. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Diagnosis: acute hematogenous osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: His 66-year-old grandfather has type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and a painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head. A sterile probe passed through the ulcer touches bone, and MRI shows osteomyelitis of the metatarsal head. Which of the following best describes how infection most likely reached the grandfather's bone?
options: Seeding of slow-flowing metaphyseal capillaries during bacteremia
Contiguous spread from the overlying soft tissue infection
Seeding of a vertebral endplate through a segmental artery
Direct inoculation of the bone during a surgical procedure
approach: Note the setting: a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer that probes to bone.
In adults with diabetes, osteomyelitis of the foot usually starts in the ulcer and spreads directly into the bone beneath it.
Contrast this with the boy, whose infection arrived through the blood and lodged in the metaphysis.
questions.why: Children usually get osteomyelitis by the hematogenous route, and bacteria lodge in the metaphysis, where looping capillaries beneath the growth plate slow blood flow. Adults more often get it by contiguous spread. In diabetes, neuropathy and poor perfusion allow a pressure ulcer to deepen until it reaches bone, and the infection is often polymicrobial. A positive probe-to-bone test strongly supports this route. Hematogenous infection in adults favors the vertebrae, where it involves two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them.
whyNot: This is the hematogenous route typical of children, like the boy in this case. The grandfather's bone lies directly under an open ulcer.
Correct.
Hematogenous vertebral osteomyelitis with discitis is the common pattern of blood-borne bone infection in adults, but the grandfather's infection is in the foot under an ulcer.
Direct inoculation occurs with surgery, open fractures, or puncture wounds. He has had no procedure at this site.

questions.stem: At 15 years of age, he fractures his right femur, which is fixed with an intramedullary nail. Three months later, the wound drains pus. Cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus that is susceptible in vitro to the antibiotic he receives, yet the infection persists until the nail is removed. Which of the following best explains this persistence?
options: Protein A binding the Fc region of IgG
Penicillin-binding protein with low drug affinity
Superantigen activation of many T cells
Growth in a biofilm on the implant surface
approach: The organism is susceptible in vitro, so drug resistance genes are not the explanation.
Infection that clears only after hardware removal points to bacteria living on the implant.
S aureus forms biofilm on metal, which shields bacteria from antibiotics and host defenses.
questions.why: S aureus attaches to implants and exposed bone matrix with adhesins for collagen and fibronectin, then grows in a biofilm, a layer of bacteria in a self-made polysaccharide and protein matrix. Bacteria in biofilm grow slowly and are protected from neutrophils and antibiotics, so drug levels that kill free-floating bacteria in the laboratory fail in the patient. This is why hardware infections often need removal of the device. Together with protein A and its adhesins, biofilm helps make S aureus the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
whyNot: Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG and blocks opsonization. It helps the organism evade phagocytosis in general but does not explain cure only after hardware removal.
An altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) gives methicillin resistance. This isolate is susceptible, so resistance is not the problem.
Superantigens such as TSST-1 cause toxic shock by activating many T cells. They do not explain a persistent local infection on hardware.
Correct.

questions.stem: Infection that starts in the marrow of the metaphysis reaches the subperiosteal space by passing through the cortex. Which of the following channels in compact bone run perpendicular to its long axis and link the marrow cavity with the periosteal surface?
options: Central canals of the osteons
Canaliculi between osteocyte lacunae
Perforating (Volkmann) canals
Resorption bays on bone surfaces
approach: Picture compact bone: osteons with central canals running along the long axis of the bone.
Channels that run across the bone and connect central canals to the marrow cavity and the periosteum are perforating (Volkmann) canals.
These vascular channels give pus a route from the marrow to the subperiosteal space.
questions.why: Compact bone is built of osteons, each made of concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal that runs parallel to the long axis and carries vessels and nerves. Perforating (Volkmann) canals run at right angles to the osteons, linking central canals with each other, with the marrow cavity, and with the periosteum. In hematogenous osteomyelitis, pus under pressure spreads from the metaphyseal marrow through these channels to lift the periosteum and form a subperiosteal abscess.
whyNot: Central (Haversian) canals run along the long axis of the bone in the center of each osteon. They do not cross the cortex.
Canaliculi are tiny channels that connect osteocytes to each other through their processes. They carry no vessels across the cortex.
Correct.
Resorption bays (Howship lacunae) are shallow pits where osteoclasts dissolve bone. They are surface features, not channels through the cortex.

questions.stem: Suppose his infection had become chronic, and a sinus tract over the tibia had drained intermittently for 30 years. A firm, ulcerated, enlarging mass then develops at the opening of the sinus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma
Secondary osteosarcoma
Basal cell carcinoma
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
approach: Identify the setting: long-standing chronic osteomyelitis with a draining sinus tract.
Chronic inflammation and repeated repair of the epithelium lining a sinus raise the risk of epithelial cancer.
The classic tumor that arises in a chronic sinus tract or scar is squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.why: Chronic osteomyelitis can leave dead bone (sequestrum), a shell of new bone (involucrum), and a sinus tract that drains to the skin for years. The squamous epithelium that grows into and around the tract undergoes constant injury and repair, and after many years squamous cell carcinoma can arise there. A new, enlarging, ulcerated mass or a change in drainage at a long-standing sinus calls for biopsy. Other late complications include amyloidosis and pathologic fracture.
whyNot: Correct.
Osteosarcoma arises after radiation or in Paget disease, and rarely after chronic infection. It would arise within bone rather than at the skin opening of a sinus.
Basal cell carcinoma usually arises on sun-exposed skin of the head and neck. It is not the tumor typical of chronic sinus tracts.
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a slow-growing dermal sarcoma of the trunk and is not linked to chronic osteomyelitis.

dx: Scaphoid waist fracture with nonunion and proximal pole avascular necrosis
case: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of persistent pain on the radial side of his right wrist. Ten months ago he fell onto his outstretched hand while snowboarding but did not seek care because the pain was mild. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. Physical examination shows tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox and pain with axial loading of the thumb. Radiographs show a fracture line through the waist of the scaphoid with sclerotic, cystic margins, and the proximal fragment is uniformly dense. MRI shows loss of normal marrow signal in the proximal pole. Diagnosis: scaphoid waist fracture with nonunion and avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the proximal fragment, rather than the distal fragment, underwent necrosis?
options: Its arterial supply enters distally and flows retrograde
It receives blood only through the scapholunate ligament
It is drained by veins that the fracture callus compresses
It lies in the territory of the ulnar artery at the wrist
approach: Recall that most of the scaphoid is covered by articular cartilage, so vessels can enter only at a few sites.
Branches of the radial artery enter at the dorsal ridge near the waist and the distal tubercle, then flow back toward the proximal pole.
A waist fracture cuts this retrograde flow, so the proximal pole loses its blood supply.
questions.why: The scaphoid gets its blood from branches of the radial artery that enter through the dorsal ridge near the waist and through the distal tubercle. The proximal pole has no direct supply and depends on blood flowing retrograde from these distal entry points. A fracture through the waist cuts off this flow, so the proximal fragment can undergo avascular necrosis and the fracture often fails to unite. The femoral neck has a similar problem, because its retinacular vessels are torn by displaced fractures.
whyNot: Correct.
The scapholunate ligament carries few vessels. The proximal pole depends on retrograde flow from the radial artery branches.
Venous compression is not the mechanism. The problem is loss of arterial inflow from the distal entry points.
The scaphoid is supplied mainly by branches of the radial artery, not the ulnar artery.

questions.stem: A year before this injury, he fractured the medial epicondyle of his left humerus. Injury to the nerve at greatest risk with that fracture would most likely cause which of the following deficits?
options: Weak wrist extension and numbness over the dorsal first web space
Weak thumb opposition and numbness over the lateral palm
Weak finger abduction and numbness over the little finger
Weak shoulder abduction and numbness over the lateral shoulder
approach: Identify the nerve that runs in the groove behind the medial epicondyle: the ulnar nerve.
The ulnar nerve supplies most intrinsic hand muscles, including the interossei that abduct and adduct the fingers.
It also carries sensation from the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger.
questions.why: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, where it is exposed to injury from fractures and direct blows. It supplies the interossei, the medial two lumbricals, and the hypothenar muscles, so injury weakens finger abduction and adduction and can cause clawing of the ring and little fingers. Sensory loss involves the little finger and the ulnar side of the ring finger. Other fracture sites have their own nerves at risk: the surgical neck of the humerus (axillary) and the radial groove of the shaft (radial).
whyNot: Weak wrist extension with dorsal web space numbness is a radial nerve injury, which is linked to fractures of the midshaft of the humerus in the radial groove.
Weak thumb opposition with lateral palm numbness is a median nerve injury, which is linked to supracondylar fractures and carpal tunnel compression.
Correct.
Weak abduction with lateral shoulder numbness is an axillary nerve injury, which is linked to fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus.

topics: Nerves at risk with humeral fractures

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how his cigarette smoking contributed to the failure of this fracture to unite?
options: Excess parathyroid hormone release dissolving the mineralized callus
Vasoconstriction and tissue hypoxia limiting callus formation
Antibodies against type II collagen destroying the soft callus
Impaired gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin in the woven bone
approach: Fracture healing needs new blood vessels to grow into the callus so cartilage can be replaced by bone.
Nicotine constricts vessels and slows new vessel growth, and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen delivery.
A bone with an already poor blood supply, like the scaphoid, is especially likely to fail to unite.
questions.why: Fracture healing moves from hematoma and inflammation to soft callus, hard callus, and remodeling, and each step depends on a good blood supply. Smoking reduces blood flow through nicotine-induced vasoconstriction, slows the growth of new vessels into the callus, and lowers oxygen delivery because carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin. The result is delayed union or nonunion, especially in bones with a fragile supply such as the scaphoid. Other factors that delay union include instability, infection, diabetes, and malnutrition.
whyNot: Smoking does not cause hyperparathyroidism, and parathyroid hormone excess is not the reason fractures fail to unite in smokers.
Correct.
There is no autoimmune attack on callus collagen in smokers.
Gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin depends on vitamin K. Smoking does not block this step, and it is not the main cause of nonunion.

topics: Causes of delayed union and nonunion

questions.stem: After bone grafting, osteoclasts resorb the dead bone of the proximal pole. Acid secreted at their ruffled border dissolves the hydroxyapatite. Which of the following enzymes do these cells secrete to degrade the exposed type I collagen?
options: Alkaline phosphatase
Carbonic anhydrase II
Lysyl oxidase
Cathepsin K
approach: Osteoclasts resorb bone in two steps: acid dissolves the mineral, then a protease digests the organic matrix.
The key collagen-digesting protease secreted into the Howship lacuna is cathepsin K.
Rule out enzymes that make acid, build collagen, or help mineralize bone.
questions.why: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells of the monocyte and macrophage lineage. They seal onto bone and form a ruffled border facing a Howship lacuna. Proton pumps acidify this space to dissolve hydroxyapatite, using protons generated by carbonic anhydrase II. The exposed type I collagen is then digested by cathepsin K, a lysosomal cysteine protease secreted into the lacuna. Osteoblasts, by contrast, make osteoid and alkaline phosphatase, and osteocytes sense load and secrete FGF23.
whyNot: Alkaline phosphatase is made by osteoblasts and promotes mineralization. It does not digest collagen.
Carbonic anhydrase II in osteoclasts makes the protons that dissolve mineral. It does not digest collagen.
Lysyl oxidase forms cross-links in newly made collagen. It strengthens collagen rather than degrading it.
Correct.

case: A 46-year-old woman is evaluated on the second day after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma because of tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips and painful cramping of her hands. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes produces flexion of the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints. Serum studies show total calcium 6.8 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), albumin 4.0 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0), phosphate 5.6 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), and PTH 4 pg/mL (10 to 65). Diagnosis: hypocalcemic tetany from postsurgical hypoparathyroidism.

questions.stem: Low extracellular calcium makes her nerves and muscles more excitable. In contrast, a man with acute kidney injury and a serum potassium concentration of 7.4 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0) has flaccid weakness of his limbs. Which of the following best explains his weakness?
options: Lower voltage threshold for sodium channel opening
Hyperpolarization of the membrane away from threshold
Sustained depolarization that inactivates sodium channels
Reduced acetylcholine release from the motor nerve terminal
approach: High extracellular potassium makes the resting membrane potential less negative.
A membrane held partly depolarized keeps many voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state.
With fewer sodium channels available, action potentials fail and muscle becomes weak despite being closer to threshold.
questions.why: Extracellular calcium normally stabilizes voltage-gated sodium channels. When calcium is low, these channels open at a less negative voltage, so nerves fire spontaneously and tetany follows, as in this patient. Hyperkalemia works differently. It depolarizes the resting membrane, and sustained depolarization closes the inactivation gates of sodium channels, so fewer are available to start an action potential. The fibers become inexcitable and weak. Hypokalemia also causes weakness, but by hyperpolarizing the membrane away from threshold.
whyNot: A lower sodium channel threshold is the mechanism of hypocalcemia, which causes hyperexcitability and tetany rather than flaccid weakness.
Hyperpolarization away from threshold is the mechanism of weakness in hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Correct.
Reduced acetylcholine release is seen with hypermagnesemia, botulism, or Lambert-Eaton syndrome. It is not how high potassium causes weakness.

questions.stem: She is treated with calcium and calcitriol rather than cholecalciferol. Which of the following best explains why she needs the active hormone?
options: Hepatic 25-hydroxylation fails without parathyroid hormone
Skin synthesis of cholecalciferol fails after neck surgery
Intestinal absorption of cholecalciferol requires thyroid hormone
Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation falls without parathyroid hormone
approach: Trace vitamin D activation: 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin, 25-hydroxylation in the liver, then 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney.
Identify the regulated step: PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
Without PTH, she cannot make enough calcitriol, so giving the precursor will not correct her calcium.
questions.why: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is made when UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin, or it is absorbed from food. The liver adds a hydroxyl group at carbon 25 in a step that is not tightly regulated, so 25-hydroxyvitamin D reflects vitamin D stores. The kidney then adds a 1-alpha hydroxyl group to make calcitriol, and this step is stimulated by PTH and low phosphate. After removal of her parathyroid glands, 1-alpha-hydroxylation falls, so she needs calcitriol itself to absorb calcium from the gut.
whyNot: Hepatic 25-hydroxylation is not regulated by PTH and continues normally in hypoparathyroidism.
Neck surgery does not affect the skin's ability to make cholecalciferol under UVB light.
Intestinal absorption of cholecalciferol depends on fat absorption with bile acids, not on thyroid hormone, and her thyroid hormone will be replaced.
Correct.

questions.stem: Tapping over the facial nerve just anterior to her ear causes twitching of her upper lip and the corner of her mouth. Which of the following muscles is supplied by the same nerve as the muscles that twitch?
options: Buccinator
Masseter
Genioglossus
Palatoglossus
approach: Recognize the Chvostek sign: tapping the facial nerve makes the muscles of facial expression twitch.
These muscles are supplied by CN VII.
Pick the muscle of facial expression: the buccinator, which is supplied by CN VII even though it lies near the muscles of mastication.
questions.why: The Chvostek sign is twitching of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped in front of the ear, and it reflects the increased nerve excitability of hypocalcemia. The muscles that twitch are muscles of facial expression, all supplied by CN VII, and the buccinator belongs to this group. The muscles of mastication, including the masseter, are supplied by CN V3. The tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII, except palatoglossus, which is supplied by CN X.
whyNot: Correct.
The masseter is a muscle of mastication supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
The genioglossus is a tongue muscle supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
The palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X) through the pharyngeal plexus.

topics: Cranial nerve supply of head and neck muscles

questions.stem: Her 72-year-old father has an enlarging skull, hearing loss, and thickened, coarse bone in the skull and pelvis on radiographs. Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely in her father?
options: Calcium high, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high
Calcium normal, phosphate normal, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH normal
Calcium low, phosphate high, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high
Calcium normal, phosphate normal, alkaline phosphatase normal, PTH normal
approach: Recognize Paget disease of bone: an older adult with skull enlargement, hearing loss, and thick, coarse bone.
Paget disease is a disorder of bone remodeling, not of calcium regulation, so calcium, phosphate, and PTH stay normal.
Intense osteoblast activity raises alkaline phosphatase, often as an isolated finding.
questions.why: In Paget disease, overactive osteoclasts are followed by disorganized osteoblast activity, which raises serum alkaline phosphatase. Because calcium and phosphate balance is not disturbed, calcium, phosphate, and PTH are usually normal. Other patterns to compare: osteoporosis has all normal values, primary hyperparathyroidism has high calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH, osteomalacia has low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, and high PTH, and renal osteodystrophy has low calcium, high phosphate, and high PTH.
whyNot: High calcium, low phosphate, and high PTH point to primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a parathyroid adenoma.
Correct.
Low calcium with high phosphate and high PTH points to renal osteodystrophy from chronic kidney disease.
Entirely normal values fit osteoporosis. Paget disease raises alkaline phosphatase because bone turnover is intense.

topics: Serum markers in metabolic bone disease

dx: Anterior cruciate ligament tear with medial meniscus and MCL injury
case: A 19-year-old woman who plays collegiate basketball is brought to the physician after injuring her left knee when another player fell against the outside of the knee while her foot was planted. She felt a pop and could not continue playing, and the knee swelled within 2 hours. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). There is a large effusion and tenderness along the medial joint line. With the knee flexed 20 to 30 degrees, the tibia moves excessively forward on the femur, and valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion opens the medial joint space. MRI shows a complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, a partial tear of the medial collateral ligament, and a tear of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. Diagnosis: anterior cruciate ligament tear with medial meniscus and MCL injury.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the medial meniscus was torn along with the MCL in this injury?
options: It is attached to the popliteus tendon, which drags it into the joint
It is fixed to the joint capsule and the deep fibers of the MCL
It is more circular and covers more of the tibial plateau surface
It is attached to the fibular collateral ligament, which tightens with valgus force
approach: A valgus blow stretches and tears the MCL on the medial side of the knee.
The medial meniscus is firmly attached to the capsule and the deep part of the MCL, so it cannot move away from the force.
The lateral meniscus is more mobile and is not attached to its collateral ligament, so it is injured less often.
questions.why: The MCL (tibial collateral ligament) has deep fibers that blend with the joint capsule and attach firmly to the medial meniscus. When a valgus force tears the MCL, the attached and relatively immobile medial meniscus is pulled and torn with it. The lateral meniscus is more circular and more mobile, is separated from the fibular collateral ligament by the popliteus tendon, and is torn less often. The ACL is tested with the anterior drawer and Lachman tests, the PCL with the posterior drawer test, the MCL with valgus stress, and the LCL with varus stress.
whyNot: The popliteus tendon attaches to the lateral meniscus, and it pulls that meniscus backward out of harm's way during knee flexion.
Correct.
This describes the lateral meniscus, which is more circular and covers more of the lateral tibial plateau.
The fibular collateral ligament is on the lateral side, is not attached to the medial meniscus, and is slack under valgus stress.

questions.stem: At 46 years of age, she has left knee pain that worsens as the day goes on and morning stiffness that lasts about 10 minutes. Which of the following radiographic findings in her left knee is most likely?
options: Medial joint space narrowing with marginal osteophytes
Uniform joint space narrowing with marginal erosions and osteopenia
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges near the joint
Linear calcification of the menisci without joint space loss
approach: Recognize post-traumatic osteoarthritis: a prior ligament and meniscal injury, pain worse with use, and brief morning stiffness.
Osteoarthritis affects weight-bearing compartments unevenly, often the medial compartment of the knee.
Its radiographic signs are asymmetric joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis and cysts.
questions.why: Osteoarthritis causes pain that worsens with use and through the day, and morning stiffness that lasts less than 30 minutes. A prior ACL tear and meniscal damage change joint mechanics and are strong risk factors. Radiographs show asymmetric joint space narrowing, most often in the medial compartment of the knee, along with osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts. In the hands, osteoarthritis produces Heberden nodes at the DIP joints and Bouchard nodes at the PIP joints.
whyNot: Correct.
Uniform narrowing with marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia is the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, which has prolonged morning stiffness.
Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges are typical of chronic tophaceous gout.
Linear calcification of the menisci (chondrocalcinosis) suggests calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.

questions.stem: Years before her radiographic changes appeared, the articular cartilage of her medial compartment began to degenerate. Which of the following is the earliest change in the cartilage matrix in this process?
options: Citrullination of collagen creating new autoantigens
Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in the matrix
Defective hydroxylation of proline in type II collagen
Proteoglycan loss with softening of the matrix
approach: Normal cartilage resists compression because aggrecan holds water in a type II collagen network.
In early osteoarthritis, chondrocytes release enzymes that degrade aggrecan first, and proteoglycan content falls.
The softened matrix then fibrillates and cracks, and later the cartilage wears away to bone.
questions.why: In osteoarthritis, injured chondrocytes release matrix metalloproteinases and aggrecanases. The earliest matrix change is loss of proteoglycan (aggrecan), with altered water content, so the cartilage softens. Next, the surface fibrillates and cracks, chondrocytes form clusters, and fragments break off into the joint. Eventually the cartilage is lost, and the exposed subchondral bone becomes sclerotic and polished (eburnation), with cysts and osteophytes.
whyNot: Citrullinated proteins are targets of anti-CCP antibodies in rheumatoid arthritis, not an early step in osteoarthritis.
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition defines CPPD disease (pseudogout). It can coexist with osteoarthritis but is not its first step.
Defective proline hydroxylation results from vitamin C deficiency (scurvy). It is not a feature of osteoarthritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: During rehabilitation, she feels sudden pain in the back of her right thigh while sprinting. MRI shows a partial tear of the biceps femoris at its musculotendinous junction, with no ligament or joint injury. Which of the following best classifies this injury?
options: Contusion
Sprain
Strain
Subluxation
approach: Identify the tissue injured: muscle and tendon at the musculotendinous junction.
Injury to muscle or tendon is a strain, while injury to a ligament is a sprain.
Eccentric loading of the hamstrings during sprinting is the classic mechanism.
questions.why: A strain is a stretch injury or tear of muscle or tendon, usually at the musculotendinous junction during forceful eccentric contraction, as when the hamstrings slow the swinging leg in a sprint. A sprain is a ligament injury, such as her earlier ACL and MCL tears. A contusion is bleeding into soft tissue from a direct blow, and a dislocation is complete loss of contact between joint surfaces (partial loss is subluxation). Ligaments heal more slowly than muscle because they have few cells and a poor blood supply.
whyNot: A contusion follows a direct blow and causes bleeding into soft tissue without a tear at the musculotendinous junction.
A sprain is an injury to a ligament, such as her ACL and MCL tears, not to muscle or tendon.
Correct.
A subluxation is partial loss of contact between joint surfaces. Her MRI shows no joint injury.

dx: Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia in a homebound older woman
case: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her daughter because of a 6-month history of aching pain in her hips, ribs, and lower back. She lives alone and has rarely left her apartment for 2 years. She eats little dairy or fish. Physical examination shows diffuse bone tenderness. Serum studies show calcium 8.3 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), phosphate 2.1 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), alkaline phosphatase 245 U/L (40 to 120), PTH 128 pg/mL (10 to 65), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 7 ng/mL (30 to 100). A pelvic radiograph shows bilateral pseudofractures of the pubic rami. Diagnosis: osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why newly formed osteoid in her skeleton fails to mineralize?
options: Osteoblasts secrete too little type I collagen
Low alkaline phosphatase leaves excess pyrophosphate
Osteoclasts cannot acidify their resorption pits
Too little calcium and phosphate for hydroxyapatite
approach: Vitamin D drives intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
In deficiency, both fall in the fluid around bone, and high PTH adds renal phosphate loss.
Without enough calcium and phosphate, hydroxyapatite cannot form in the osteoid, which stays unmineralized.
questions.why: Bone mineral is hydroxyapatite, which forms in osteoid only when the local calcium and phosphate concentrations are high enough. Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal absorption of both, and the secondary hyperparathyroidism it causes increases urinary phosphate loss. Osteoblasts keep laying down osteoid, but it does not mineralize, so bone is soft and wide seams of osteoid build up. Before growth plate closure this causes rickets, and after closure it causes osteomalacia.
whyNot: Osteoblasts make osteoid normally in osteomalacia. The defect is in mineralizing it, not in making collagen.
Low alkaline phosphatase with excess pyrophosphate is the mechanism of hypophosphatasia. Her alkaline phosphatase is high.
Failure of osteoclasts to acidify resorption pits causes osteopetrosis, which produces dense bone rather than unmineralized bone.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her medications include phenytoin for a seizure disorder, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, amlodipine for hypertension, and metformin for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which of these drugs most likely contributed to her vitamin D deficiency?
options: Amlodipine
Levothyroxine
Phenytoin
Metformin
approach: List the risk factors for vitamin D deficiency: little sun, darker skin, fat malabsorption, liver or kidney disease, and anticonvulsants.
Phenytoin induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes.
These enzymes convert vitamin D and 25-hydroxyvitamin D to inactive products, lowering her stores further.
questions.why: Her main risk factor is lack of sun, because UVB light on the skin is the major source of vitamin D, and older skin makes less of it. Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, phenobarbital, and carbamazepine induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that speed the breakdown of vitamin D to inactive metabolites. Other risk factors include darker skin, unsupplemented exclusive breastfeeding in infants, fat malabsorption, and liver or kidney disease.
whyNot: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker that does not affect vitamin D metabolism.
Excess levothyroxine can speed bone turnover and cause osteoporosis, but it does not cause vitamin D deficiency.
Correct.
Long-term metformin use can lower vitamin B12 absorption, not vitamin D.

topics: Risk factors for vitamin D deficiency

questions.stem: She has difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs, and she walks with a waddling gait. Serum creatine kinase is 64 U/L (30 to 170). Which of the following best explains her weakness?
options: T cell-mediated injury of the proximal muscle fibers
Muscle dysfunction from low vitamin D and phosphate
Inflammatory bursitis of the shoulders and hips
Type II fiber atrophy from glucocorticoid excess
approach: Note proximal weakness with a normal creatine kinase, which argues against muscle fiber necrosis.
Osteomalacia commonly causes proximal muscle weakness and a waddling gait along with bone pain.
Low vitamin D action in muscle and low phosphate impair muscle function, and treatment reverses it.
questions.why: Osteomalacia classically causes diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness with a waddling gait, and Looser zones (pseudofractures). The weakness comes from reduced vitamin D signaling in muscle and from hypophosphatemia, which limits ATP production, and creatine kinase stays normal because fibers are not destroyed. Her labs fit the usual pattern: low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Replacement of vitamin D usually restores strength.
whyNot: T cell injury of muscle fibers occurs in polymyositis, which raises creatine kinase. Her creatine kinase is normal.
Correct.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes pain and stiffness of the shoulders and hips with high inflammatory markers, not the bone pain and abnormal mineral labs she has.
Glucocorticoid myopathy causes type II fiber atrophy, but she is not taking glucocorticoids, and her labs point to vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: Her 68-year-old neighbor has taken prednisone 15 mg daily for 4 years for asthma and sustains a vertebral compression fracture. A lumbar spine T-score is minus 2.9. Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are normal. Which of the following best explains the neighbor's bone loss?
options: Suppressed osteoblast formation of new bone
Defective mineralization of newly formed osteoid
Osteoclast activation by excess parathyroid hormone
Abnormal type I collagen from a COL1A1 mutation
approach: Normal mineral labs with low bone density mean osteoporosis: less bone that is normally mineralized.
Long-term glucocorticoids are the most common secondary cause.
Their main effect is to suppress osteoblast formation and survival, so too little new bone is made.
questions.why: Osteoporosis is reduced bone mass with normal mineralization, so serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH are usually normal. Glucocorticoids cause bone loss mainly by suppressing osteoblast formation and promoting osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis, and they also raise RANKL and reduce calcium absorption. Other drivers of osteoporosis include low peak bone mass, estrogen loss, aging, hyperthyroidism, immobilization, alcohol, and smoking.
whyNot: Correct.
Defective mineralization is osteomalacia, which would show low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, and often low vitamin D.
Excess PTH points to hyperparathyroidism. Her neighbor's PTH and calcium are normal.
COL1A1 mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta, which presents with fractures from childhood, not after years of prednisone.

dx: Osteosarcoma of the proximal tibia in a teenager with Li-Fraumeni syndrome
case: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain below his left knee that now wakes him at night. His mother had breast cancer at 34 years of age, and his maternal uncle died of a soft tissue sarcoma at 25 years of age. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). Physical examination shows a firm, tender mass over the proximal medial tibia. Radiographs show a destructive lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with a sunburst pattern of periosteal bone and a Codman triangle. Chest CT shows no nodules. Germline testing shows a pathogenic TP53 variant. Diagnosis: osteosarcoma of the proximal tibia in Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

questions.stem: A biopsy specimen of the mass is examined. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Pleomorphic cells producing lacelike tumor osteoid
Sheets of small round blue cells with membranous CD99
Malignant chondrocytes in hyaline matrix without osteoid
Mononuclear stromal cells among osteoclast-like giant cells
approach: Recognize osteosarcoma: an adolescent with a metaphyseal tumor near the knee, a sunburst pattern, and a Codman triangle.
Osteosarcoma is defined by malignant cells that make osteoid.
Rule out tumors defined by other cell types: small round cells, cartilage, or giant cells.
questions.why: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor apart from multiple myeloma. It arises most often in the metaphysis around the knee and peaks in adolescence, with a second peak in older adults with Paget disease or prior radiation. The defining finding is pleomorphic malignant cells that produce osteoid, often in a lacelike pattern. Tumor bone lifting the periosteum makes the Codman triangle, and spicules radiating outward make the sunburst pattern.
whyNot: Correct.
Small round blue cells with membranous CD99 describe Ewing sarcoma, which favors the diaphysis and pelvis and gives an onion-skin periosteal reaction.
Malignant chondrocytes without tumor osteoid describe chondrosarcoma, which usually affects older adults in the pelvis and proximal femur.
Stromal cells with osteoclast-like giant cells describe giant cell tumor of bone, an epiphyseal tumor of young adults after growth plate closure.

topics: Primary bone tumors by age and site

questions.stem: Which of the following normal functions of the protein encoded by his mutated gene best explains his susceptibility to this and other cancers?
options: Binding E2F to hold cells in G1 until growth signals arrive
Halting the cell cycle through p21 after DNA damage
Inactivating RAS by stimulating its GTPase activity
Repairing base mismatches left after DNA replication
approach: Identify the gene: TP53, the cause of Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
Recall that p53 senses DNA damage and induces p21, which blocks cyclin-dependent kinases and halts the cell at G1.
Without p53, damaged cells keep dividing and avoid apoptosis, so mutations accumulate and many tumors arise early.
questions.why: p53 is a transcription factor that rises after DNA damage. It turns on p21, which inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and stops the cell at the G1 checkpoint so the DNA can be repaired, and it triggers apoptosis through BAX if the damage cannot be fixed. People with Li-Fraumeni syndrome inherit one defective TP53 copy, and loss of the second copy in a cell removes this checkpoint. They develop sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma at young ages. Osteosarcoma also spreads through the blood, most often to the lungs.
whyNot: Holding cells in G1 by binding E2F is the function of the RB protein. RB1 loss causes retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, but his mutated gene is TP53.
Correct.
Stimulating RAS GTPase activity is the function of neurofibromin (NF1), not p53.
Mismatch repair is carried out by MLH1, MSH2, and related proteins, which are defective in Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: The tumor has spread into the surrounding soft tissue but has not crossed the articular cartilage into the knee joint. During development, which of the following processes formed the cavity of this joint?
options: Regression of the apical ectodermal ridge
Resorption of the secondary ossification center
Cavitation of the interzone mesenchyme
Fusion of adjacent halves of two sclerotomes
approach: Recall that limb bones begin as continuous condensations of mesenchyme that become cartilage models.
Where a joint will form, a band of dense mesenchyme called the interzone stays between the cartilage models.
Cells in the interzone die or spread apart to open the joint cavity, a process called cavitation.
questions.why: Synovial joints form where the mesenchyme between two developing cartilage models condenses into an interzone. The central interzone cavitates to form the joint cavity, while its outer layers form the capsule, synovium, ligaments, and in the knee the menisci. The long bones themselves form by endochondral ossification, with a primary center in the diaphysis and secondary centers in the epiphyses, while the flat bones of the skull vault and most of the clavicle form by intramembranous ossification.
whyNot: The apical ectodermal ridge drives outgrowth of the limb bud along its proximal to distal axis. It does not form joint cavities.
Secondary ossification centers form bone in the epiphyses. They are not resorbed to create the joint cavity.
Correct.
Fusion of adjacent sclerotome halves forms the vertebral bodies, not the joints of the limbs.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, he recalled being kicked in the calf during a soccer game 6 weeks earlier, and myositis ossificans was considered. In myositis ossificans, which of the following best explains the bone that forms within the muscle?
options: Dystrophic calcification of necrotic skeletal muscle fibers
Metastatic calcification of muscle from high serum calcium
Malignant osteoblasts invading the muscle from adjacent bone
Mesenchymal cells in injured muscle becoming osteoblasts
approach: Myositis ossificans follows muscle trauma and contains true bone, not just calcium deposits.
Mesenchymal progenitor cells in the injured muscle are signaled to become osteoblasts.
The process matures from the outside in, so mature bone forms at the periphery of the lesion.
questions.why: Myositis ossificans is heterotopic ossification in muscle after trauma. Mesenchymal progenitor cells in the damaged tissue, responding to local signals such as bone morphogenetic proteins, differentiate into osteoblasts and lay down true bone. The lesion matures in zones: proliferating fibroblast-like cells in the center and mature lamellar bone at the periphery. Osteosarcoma shows the opposite pattern, with the most mature and densest tumor bone near its center and immature cells at its edges.
whyNot: Dystrophic calcification deposits calcium salts in dead tissue but does not form organized bone with osteoblasts and lamellae.
Metastatic calcification requires high serum calcium or phosphate. He has no such disorder, and it does not produce true bone.
Invasion by malignant osteoblasts describes a bone sarcoma spreading into muscle, not a reactive process after injury.
Correct.

dx: Pelvic Ewing sarcoma in an adolescent
case: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain in her right buttock and hip, intermittent fever, and a 3-kg weight loss. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F). There is a firm, tender mass over the right iliac wing. Leukocyte count is 12,600/mm3 (4,500 to 13,000), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 58 mm/h (0 to 20). CT shows a permeative, destructive lesion of the right ilium extending to the acetabulum with a large soft tissue mass. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells with membranous CD99 staining, and molecular testing shows a t(11;22) translocation. Diagnosis: Ewing sarcoma of the pelvis.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, her fever and high sedimentation rate had suggested osteomyelitis. Which of the following findings on plain radiographs would have favored her tumor?
options: Spiculated sunburst pattern radiating from the bone
Thin expansile shell around a soap-bubble lesion
Layered new bone in an onion-skin pattern
Dense sclerosis around a small lucent nidus
approach: Note that Ewing sarcoma can cause fever, leukocytosis, and a high sedimentation rate, so it mimics osteomyelitis.
Ewing sarcoma grows in waves and repeatedly lifts the periosteum.
Each lift lays down a new layer of bone, giving the onion-skin pattern.
questions.why: Ewing sarcoma is a tumor of children and adolescents that arises in the diaphysis of long bones or in the pelvis. It is made of small round blue cells that express CD99 and carry the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion from t(11;22). Because it can cause fever, leukocytosis, and a high sedimentation rate, it is often mistaken for osteomyelitis. Its radiographic hallmark is a permeative lesion with layered, onion-skin periosteal new bone, and biopsy settles the diagnosis.
whyNot: A sunburst pattern with spicules radiating from the bone is typical of osteosarcoma.
An expansile soap-bubble lesion is typical of giant cell tumor of bone in the epiphysis of young adults.
Correct.
A small lucent nidus surrounded by dense sclerosis is typical of osteoid osteoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the structure of the oncoprotein produced by her translocation?
options: EWSR1 activation domain joined to the FLI1 DNA-binding domain
FLI1 coding sequence placed next to an immunoglobulin enhancer
Tyrosine kinase domain held active by an EWSR1 dimerization domain
Truncated FLI1 protein lacking its nuclear localization signal
approach: Identify the partners of t(11;22): EWSR1 on chromosome 22 and FLI1 on chromosome 11.
FLI1 is an ETS family transcription factor that binds DNA, and EWSR1 contributes a strong transcriptional activation domain.
The fusion is an aberrant transcription factor that turns on genes that drive tumor growth.
questions.why: In Ewing sarcoma, t(11;22)(q24;q12) fuses the 5' part of EWSR1 to the 3' part of FLI1. The fusion protein carries the activation domain of EWSR1 and the ETS DNA-binding domain of FLI1, so it binds FLI1 target sites and strongly changes the expression of many genes. Other sarcomas have different genetic drivers: osteosarcoma is linked to loss of RB1 (after hereditary retinoblastoma) or TP53 (Li-Fraumeni syndrome), and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma to PAX3 or PAX7 fused to FOXO1.
whyNot: Correct.
Placing a gene next to an immunoglobulin enhancer is how MYC is overexpressed in Burkitt lymphoma with t(8;14), not how Ewing sarcoma forms.
A constitutively active tyrosine kinase fusion describes BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia. EWSR1-FLI1 is a transcription factor, not a kinase.
The fusion keeps the DNA-binding domain of FLI1 and acts in the nucleus. A truncated protein unable to enter the nucleus would not drive the tumor.

questions.stem: Resection of her tumor requires removal of the entire right acetabulum. Which of the following bones contribute to the acetabulum?
options: Ilium and ischium, but not the pubis
Ilium and pubis, but not the ischium
Ischium and pubis, but not the ilium
Ilium, ischium, and pubis
approach: Recall that each hip bone forms from three bones: ilium, ischium, and pubis.
In childhood they are joined by a Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage in the floor of the acetabulum.
All three fuse there in the mid-teens, so all three form part of the acetabulum.
questions.why: The hip bone develops from three separate bones, the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. Until the mid-teens they are joined by a Y-shaped triradiate cartilage in the acetabular floor, and then they fuse. The ilium forms the upper part of the acetabulum, the ischium the posteroinferior part, and the pubis the anterior part. Resection of the whole acetabulum therefore removes part of all three bones.
whyNot: The pubis forms the anterior part of the acetabulum, so it cannot be left out.
The ischium forms the posteroinferior part of the acetabulum, so it cannot be left out.
The ilium forms the upper, weight-bearing part of the acetabulum, so it cannot be left out.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has rapidly progressive proptosis of his left eye from an orbital mass. Whole-body imaging shows no other lesions. Biopsy shows small round blue cells, the same broad category as her tumor. Which of the following findings in the boy's biopsy is most likely?
options: Membranous CD99 with an EWSR1-FLI1 fusion
Nuclear myogenin in cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm
Homer-Wright rosettes with neuron-specific enolase
Lymphoblasts with nuclear terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase
approach: A primary orbital mass in a young child is classic for rhabdomyosarcoma, the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is made of rhabdomyoblasts, tumor cells showing skeletal muscle differentiation.
These cells express desmin and the nuclear muscle transcription factor myogenin.
questions.why: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. It arises most often in the head and neck, including the orbit, and in the genitourinary tract, where the embryonal type can form grape-like sarcoma botryoides. The tumor cells are rhabdomyoblasts with eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes with cross-striations, and they stain for desmin and nuclear myogenin or MyoD1. The alveolar type, more common in the limbs of adolescents, carries a PAX3 or PAX7 fusion with FOXO1.
whyNot: Membranous CD99 with EWSR1-FLI1 is Ewing sarcoma, like her tumor. It usually arises in bone, not as a primary orbital soft tissue mass.
Correct.
Homer-Wright rosettes suggest neuroblastoma, which can spread to the orbit, but it would come from a primary tumor such as the adrenal medulla, and imaging shows no other lesion.
Lymphoblasts positive for terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase suggest lymphoblastic leukemia or lymphoma, not a primary soft tissue sarcoma.

dx: Cleidocranial dysplasia with retained primary teeth
case: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his primary teeth have not fallen out and his permanent teeth have not erupted. He is at the 8th percentile for height. Physical examination shows frontal bossing, a palpable open anterior fontanelle, and drooping shoulders that he can bring together in front of his chest until they nearly touch. Dental radiographs show retained primary teeth and multiple unerupted supernumerary teeth. A chest radiograph shows absence of the lateral thirds of both clavicles. His father has similar shoulder findings. Diagnosis: cleidocranial dysplasia.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a heterozygous loss-of-function variant. Which of the following best explains his skeletal findings?
options: Reduced SOX9 dosage limiting chondrocyte differentiation
Reduced RUNX2 dosage limiting osteoblast differentiation
Constitutive FGFR3 signaling limiting chondrocyte proliferation
Altered HOX gene expression changing skeletal segment identity
approach: Recognize cleidocranial dysplasia: absent clavicles, open fontanelles, and dental anomalies, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
Its cause is haploinsufficiency of RUNX2, the master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation.
One working copy makes too little RUNX2, so bones formed directly by osteoblasts are most affected.
questions.why: RUNX2 (also called CBFA1) is the master transcription factor that turns mesenchymal cells into osteoblasts. In cleidocranial dysplasia, one copy is lost, and half the normal amount is not enough (haploinsufficiency). Bones that form by intramembranous ossification, such as the clavicles and skull vault, are hit hardest, and tooth eruption is also disturbed. Other skeletal transcription factors have different roles: SOX9 drives chondrocyte differentiation, and HOX genes set segment identity.
whyNot: SOX9 drives chondrocyte differentiation, and its loss causes campomelic dysplasia with bowed long bones and often sex reversal, not absent clavicles.
Correct.
Constitutive FGFR3 signaling is a gain-of-function mechanism that causes achondroplasia, not a loss-of-function disorder of the clavicles.
HOX mutations change the identity of body segments or digits, as in synpolydactyly. They do not cause absent clavicles and open fontanelles.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his clavicles and skull vault are affected much more than the length of his limb bones?
options: They grow in length at epiphyseal growth plates
They form from a hyaline cartilage model
They arise entirely from somitic sclerotome
They ossify directly within mesenchyme
approach: Compare the two ways bone forms: intramembranous (directly from mesenchyme) and endochondral (by replacing a cartilage model).
The skull vault and most of the clavicle form by intramembranous ossification, which depends directly on osteoblast differentiation.
Limb bones grow in length by endochondral ossification at the growth plates, which depends mainly on chondrocytes.
questions.why: In intramembranous ossification, mesenchymal cells differentiate straight into osteoblasts, which lay down bone without a cartilage stage. The flat bones of the skull vault and most of the clavicle form this way. In endochondral ossification, bone replaces a hyaline cartilage model, starting at a primary center in the diaphysis and later at secondary centers in the epiphyses, and growth plates add length. Because RUNX2 deficiency limits osteoblast formation, bones made directly by osteoblasts are most affected, while limb length, set by growth plate chondrocytes, is less affected.
whyNot: Growth in length at epiphyseal plates is how limb bones lengthen. That is the process that is relatively spared in his disorder.
A hyaline cartilage model is the basis of endochondral ossification, which forms the limb bones, not the skull vault or most of the clavicle.
The skull vault comes largely from neural crest and paraxial mesoderm, and the clavicle does not come from sclerotome. Embryonic source does not explain the pattern.
Correct.

questions.stem: Because of his short stature and frontal bossing, achondroplasia was considered before his radiographs were obtained. Which of the following sets of findings would have supported achondroplasia?
options: Macrocephaly, normal trunk, normal intelligence
Microcephaly, short trunk, intellectual disability
Macrocephaly, short trunk, intellectual disability
Normal head size, short trunk, normal intelligence
approach: Recall that achondroplasia affects bones that grow by endochondral ossification at growth plates.
The limbs are short, especially the proximal segments, while the trunk is near normal in length.
The skull vault forms by intramembranous ossification and is large, with frontal bossing, and intelligence is normal.
questions.why: Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia. Endochondral growth is slowed, so the limbs are short (rhizomelic, most marked in the upper arms and thighs) while the trunk is close to normal length. The skull vault, which forms by intramembranous ossification, grows normally and looks large next to a small skull base and midface, giving macrocephaly with frontal bossing. Intelligence is normal, although narrowing of the foramen magnum can compress the brainstem in infancy.
whyNot: Correct.
Achondroplasia causes macrocephaly with a near-normal trunk, and intelligence is normal.
The head is large in achondroplasia, but the trunk is near normal in length and intelligence is normal.
Head size is increased and the trunk is near normal in achondroplasia. A short trunk suggests a spinal dysplasia.

questions.stem: In achondroplasia, the long bones are short while their width, which comes from periosteal bone formation, is nearly normal. Which of the following best explains the short long bones?
options: Loss of FGFR3 signaling that normally drives chondrocyte growth
Haploinsufficiency of a transcription factor for osteoblasts
Excess FGFR3 signaling that slows chondrocyte proliferation
Defective type II collagen in the growth plate cartilage matrix
approach: Long bones grow in length at the growth plate by chondrocyte proliferation followed by endochondral ossification.
Width comes from periosteal (intramembranous) bone formation, which is spared.
FGFR3 normally brakes chondrocyte proliferation, and gain-of-function mutations make this brake too strong.
questions.why: FGFR3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase that normally slows chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy in the growth plate. In achondroplasia, a gain-of-function mutation (usually G380R) keeps the receptor active, so growth plate chondrocytes divide too little and long bones stay short. Periosteal growth in width and intramembranous bone are spared. Most cases are new autosomal dominant mutations that arise in the father's germ line and become more common with advanced paternal age.
whyNot: FGFR3 normally inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, and achondroplasia is caused by too much FGFR3 activity, not too little.
Haploinsufficiency of the osteoblast transcription factor RUNX2 causes cleidocranial dysplasia, which mainly affects intramembranous bone.
Correct.
Defective type II collagen causes other skeletal dysplasias such as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, which typically shortens the trunk.
